analysis.one_liner: Toughened penalties for manipulating energy markets and put federal oversight on energy derivatives trading.
analysis.headline: Introduced with eight bipartisan cosponsors in March 2003, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; its only action was referral to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised criminal penalties for manipulating wholesale electricity and natural gas markets roughly two-hundred-fold, freed federal energy regulators to investigate without clearance from the Office of Management and Budget, and given the Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over off-exchange energy derivatives that had been largely exempt from regulation since 2000. It also would have extended consumer refunds when a utility's overcharge involved fraud. The bill never moved past its first day: it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on March 4, 2003, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity and natural gas bills benefit if the bill passes: higher criminal and civil penalties and stronger investigative power give regulators real leverage against price manipulation of the kind seen during the 2000-01 western energy crisis, and fraud-tainted overcharges become refundable back to the date they began. Retail and institutional buyers of energy also gain transparency and anti-fraud rules on the off-exchange derivatives markets where energy prices are set.

how_it_helps.text: Raises criminal penalties under the Federal Power Act and Natural Gas Act from a $5,000 fine and two years in prison to a $1 million fine and five years, and raises per-day fines from $500 to $50,000 — making it materially riskier for a trader or utility to manipulate energy prices [S3].

Makes price manipulation of any commodity traded under the Commodity Exchange Act a felony carrying up to 10 years in prison and up to a $1 million fine per violation, and lets the CFTC seek civil penalties of up to $1 million or triple the manipulator's gain [S2] [S3].

Frees FERC's investigative authority — its power to summon records and witnesses — from any requirement to get the consent of the Office of Management and Budget or another federal agency, so enforcement can no longer be slowed by another office [S2] [S3].

Extends the refund window for unjust utility rates: when a complaint could not have been brought earlier because of fraud or misrepresentation by the utility, refunds reach back to the date the overcharged rate took effect, instead of a fixed window [S3].

Puts basic oversight on off-exchange energy derivatives: CFTC may set core principles requiring trading platforms and dealer markets to monitor trading to prevent fraud and price distortion, keep books and records open to regulators for five years, and report large positions [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Energy traders, merchant energy companies, and derivatives dealers bear the cost: a new felony for price manipulation carrying up to 10 years in prison, civil penalties up to $1 million or triple the gain, per-day fines raised from $500 to $50,000, and recordkeeping and monitoring obligations on off-exchange energy derivatives platforms. Regulated utilities could also owe refunds stretching back to the original date of a fraudulent overcharge.

drawbacks.text: The same bill would let FERC's chairman hire consultants without following federal procurement law and, if he deems it in the public interest, without conflicts-of-interest rules — weakening ethics safeguards even as it tightens enforcement elsewhere.

Section 8 states that the anti-fraud prohibitions create no legal duty for parties trading on registered markets to give counterparties or other participants material market information, which narrows one avenue for challenging opaque dealing.

Much of the new oversight of energy derivatives is discretionary — the CFTC may impose recordkeeping, reporting, and monitoring requirements only 'to the extent the Commission determines appropriate' — so the bill's bite would have depended heavily on future regulators.
Higher penalties and expanded compliance obligations on energy traders and derivatives platforms would carry costs that businesses could pass through to the customers the bill aims to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For everyday customers of electricity and natural gas, the benefits were real and the costs were mostly borne elsewhere: bigger criminal and civil penalties for manipulation, a federal energy watchdog that could investigate without White House budget-office clearance, refunds that could reach back to the original overcharge when fraud was involved, and — through the derivatives provisions — a partial closing of the regulatory gap that let energy trading on exempt commodities escape the Commodity Exchange Act. The costs fell on energy traders and derivatives dealers in compliance and exposure, some of which could theoretically reach customers through fees. The bill's own weak points are real: Section 6 lets FERC's chairman hire consultants exempt from ordinary conflicts-of-interest laws [S3], Section 8 specifies that fraud rules impose no duty on parties on registered markets to share material market information with counterparties [S2] [S3], and much of the new derivatives oversight is only what the CFTC "determines appropriate," leaving its strength to future regulators [S3]. On balance it was a modest, bipartisan tightening of enforcement that died without ever being weighed on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on March 4, 2003, joined by six original cosponsors — two Republicans and four other Democrats [S1] [S3].
The bill finished with eight cosponsors: six Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
Its only recorded action was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on March 4, 2003; no further action was ever taken [S1] [S5].
The 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005, and the bill died in committee with no recorded vote, no floor debate, and no committee report [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy traders, merchant energy companies, and derivatives dealers were better off, because none of the new criminal penalties, manipulation fines, or oversight of off-exchange energy trading ever took effect. Electricity and gas customers gained nothing from a bill no one ever voted on.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on March 4, 2003.

against.name: Sen. Thad Cochran
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, he never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill's only recorded action was the referral and it died there.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — 6 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 51 Senate Republicans cosponsored — but the bill was never voted on, so there is no roll-call record of who supported or opposed it.

industries.industry: Energy traders and merchant energy companies
industries.note: The bill would have made energy price manipulation a felony carrying up to 10 years in prison, raised civil penalties to $1 million or triple the gain, and freed FERC to investigate without clearance from the budget office. Anyone trading power or gas contracts would have faced far more personal and corporate risk.

industries.industry: Energy derivatives dealers and off-exchange trading platforms
industries.note: Off-exchange energy derivatives had been largely exempt from the Commodity Exchange Act; the bill would have subjected covered platforms and dealer markets to anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules, five-year recordkeeping open to regulators, and possible core-principle requirements. Their gain from light-touch rules would have come at the expense of price transparency for customers.

industries.industry: Regulated electric and natural gas utilities
industries.note: Criminal fines would rise from $5,000 to $1 million and per-day penalties from $500 to $50,000, and a utility that committed fraud could be ordered to refund overcharges back to the day the rate took effect. A utility's interest in avoiding these penalties ran against customers' interest in recovering them.
